Messages.Author: Dog
Messages.Body:
I'm afraid the 7/7 rulings are the final nail in the coffin.
The rules-team can't be trusted to make rulings.

The claim which has ultimately led us here is that the game was designed to
be played 'unlimited'.
This is ridiculous.
Jyhad hasn't been designed with **anywhere near** the care and balance
necessary to achieve this!

Let's take a look at just 2 of the stunning rulings which have been
necessitated by this money-grubbing farce...

1. The No-Repeat rulings:
Let's call them what they really are...
No repeat BLEED rulings!
Anson can call conservative agitation, then kine resources contested.
But he can't bleed with legal manipulations, then with computer hacking.
i.e. 'Bleed actions' are a class, but politicals aren't
It's can't be inferred from the rulebook (unless you're a Malkie)
It's purely because the unlimited game is unbalanced by repeat-bleeding.
Experience shows that with a card limit this indefensible ruling (which
hurts many good decks) is unnecessary.

2. The incredible 7/7 edits:
Surely ALL of these cards can't be broken?
We've been playing pulled fangs for half a decade, AND NOW IT'S TOO
POWERFUL???
Yeah.
Right.
With a card-limit none of these cards is broken.

It's my impression that advocates of no-limit most often:
1. Make money from the industry, and are thus only interested in increasing
sales
2. Have a large collection, and wish to increase the benefit of that
advantage in tournament play

I dislike *any* kind of limit on our game, but the rulings which must
result from unlimited decks are vastly more restrictive than a simple card
limit could ever be!

I'd really appreciate reasoned responses from any advocates of no-limits,
if you're in the industry please admit it.
Jyhad is NOT played by morons.
Players should be able to decide for themselves if the unlimited position
can be defended, or if it's a marketing ploy and should be discarded for
our better enjoyment of the game.
If there's support I want this to be a starting place to challenge the
international tournament rules.

In an attempt to stave off claims I'm some whining brat here's a little
background...

My job is travel. I've played Jyhad in cities & towns dotted around
Australasia.
In the last 5 years I've run 17 weekend tournaments, the biggest involved
34 players
I've got a modest collection of about 30000 cards
The card limited games I've played range from 4x-6x
My preference is 5x (Vamps & uniques too, encourages theme decks)

The above comments are on the basis of thousands of card-limited games
against rabid Jyhad nutters.

Peace, Mung Beans, and an appropriately violent game of Jyhad

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On 28 Aug 1998, Dog wrote:

> I'm afraid the 7/7 rulings are the final nail in the coffin.
> The rules-team can't be trusted to make rulings.
>
> The claim which has ultimately led us here is that the game was designed to
> be played 'unlimited'.
> This is ridiculous.
> Jyhad hasn't been designed with **anywhere near** the care and balance
> necessary to achieve this!

So you are saying playing Jyhad without card limits cannot be achieved? I
think all the people who play without card limits would tend to disagree
with you.

Perhaps you should revise your claim to something more moderate, like "I
think card limits are better." Many will disagree with you, but at least
you will not sound insane.

> Let's take a look at just 2 of the stunning rulings which have been
> necessitated by this money-grubbing farce...
>
> 1. The No-Repeat rulings:

These are optional, and are only mandatory in tournament play.

> Let's call them what they really are...
> No repeat BLEED rulings!

You could call them that, but you would be wrong, and you would mislead
anyone unfortunate enough to presume you knew what you were talking about.

> Anson can call conservative agitation, then kine resources contested.

No he cannot. Calling a vote is an "action type" as defined in the
rulebook. Thus, a single minion cannot call more than one in a turn if
you are playing under NRA (No Repeat Actions).

> But he can't bleed with legal manipulations, then with computer hacking.

Correct.

> i.e. 'Bleed actions' are a class, but politicals aren't

They are both an action type. Action types are as follows:
- Hunt
- Rectruit ally
- Employ retainer
- Call a vote
- Bleed
- Leave torpor
- Diablerize vampire in torpor
- Rescue vampire from torpor
- Equip
- Transfer Equipment

> It's can't be inferred from the rulebook (unless you're a Malkie)

You are right. This is not in the rulebook. No-one has ever pretended it
was. These are tournament-only rules that many people play as house
rules.

> It's purely because the unlimited game is unbalanced by repeat-bleeding.

Repeat bleeding, which you seem to concede is a problem, is not a problem
that can be solved by card limits. There are too many different varieties
of bleed cards. And it is the Ventrue (the guys with Freak Drive and
Majesty Untap) who have access to the greatest variety of bleed-boost
cards: Threats, Conditioning, Bonding, Aire of Elation, Computer Hacking,
Govern the Unalighned, Social Charm, Legal Manipulations...to name about
half of them.

> Experience shows that with a card limit this indefensible ruling (which
> hurts many good decks) is unnecessary.

What experience showed you that?
I will agree with you partially, and say that I think it is somewhat of a
shame that the ruling limits Equipment, Retainer, and Ally based decks,
since these do not need limiting.

However, it does not limit them much, especially as permanent resource
decks can combine Equipment, Retainrs and Allies so as to make maximum use
of repeat actions. Since the rule limits vote and bleed decks MORE, then
the overall effect of the rule is to benefit these decks.

> 2. The incredible 7/7 edits:
> Surely ALL of these cards can't be broken?
> We've been playing pulled fangs for half a decade, AND NOW IT'S TOO
> POWERFUL???
> Yeah.
> Right.

Well, yeah. I mean, the card is not so powerful as to make the game
unplayable, but it does show up with nauseating frequency in combat decks,
such that the variety of the game is hurt. This would be true even with 5
card limit. Now that the card is fixed, and no longer undeniably better
than other combat cards and strategies, we may see more variety in
competitive play.

> With a card-limit none of these cards is broken.

Would you include RTI in this?

> It's my impression that advocates of no-limit most often:
> 1. Make money from the industry, and are thus only interested in increasing
> sales

I don't make money off the industry. Neither, however, do I want to see
the game die, as I love the game.

> 2. Have a large collection, and wish to increase the benefit of that
> advantage in tournament play

Yes, I admit that I am the type of person who likes to make wierd decks
like my "Bring out the Clan" nosferatu deck, which contains 11 copies of
Kindred Intelligence and 8 copies of 4th tradition. Or my Blood Doll/Baby
Factory/Cryptic Mission deck, which contains about 25 copies of Cryptic
Mission, 8 copies of Embrace, and 10 Thaumaturgy skill cards. Or my Deep
Stealth Pure Obfuscate Bleed deck, with 10 copies each of Night Moves and
Spying Mission. Sometimes, however, I like to construct "Surprise" decks,
with only one of any single card so my opponents never know what to
expect. I like having all these options.

However, I don't like using multiples of those cards that everyone likes
to abuse, since this is boring for me, and makes me feel less deserving of
victory. Even 5 of an overpowered card in my deck can give me an unfair
advantage over someone who has less than 5 of any particular power rare.
I do not even play with Wakes that much, because I am so tired of seeing
everyone else do it. I would prefer that cards be balanced, so that a
greater variety of cards from the set see regular play.

It does not seem nearly as unfair that having alot of cards gives me a
greater variety strategic options in deck design than those with fewer
cards, as long as their (less numerous) options are competitive and
viable. As long as reasonable balance of card power is maintained, this
will generally be the situation.

> I dislike *any* kind of limit on our game, but the rulings which must
> result from unlimited decks are vastly more restrictive than a simple card
> limit could ever be!

You must be joking. Even if the "fixed" cards were banned completely you
would still have about a thousand different card types to choose from when
you construct your decks. We are talking a small handful of cards out of
a huge variety of cards available. I am guessing that you must play with
these cards constantly if you are under the delusion that they are the
only ones that exist.

> I'd really appreciate reasoned responses from any advocates of no-limits,
> if you're in the industry please admit it.

I admit I am not in the industry. I own a large collection of Jyhad
cards, because they are cheapest, but from the other sets I do not have
too many. I do not have many broken cards at all, because they come mainly
from the later sets.

> Jyhad is NOT played by morons.

I agree wholeheartedly, but I am wondering why you are trying to make a
fool of yourself with this unreasoned post.

> Players should be able to decide for themselves if the unlimited position
> can be defended, or if it's a marketing ploy and should be discarded for
> our better enjoyment of the game.

Nobody is stopping any player from making their own decisions. I've made
mine, and, though it may be delusion :), I do not feel I have been
brainwashed by WOTC.

> If there's support I want this to be a starting place to challenge the
> international tournament rules.

I'm sorry, but you won't get my support on this.

> In an attempt to stave off claims I'm some whining brat here's a little
> background...
>
> My job is travel. I've played Jyhad in cities & towns dotted around
> Australasia.
> In the last 5 years I've run 17 weekend tournaments, the biggest involved
> 34 players
> I've got a modest collection of about 30000 cards

That's enough cards that many creative options will be limited by the 5
card limit, (since you will have far more than 5 of most commons) while
you still have far less than a full complement of power rares.

> The card limited games I've played range from 4x-6x
> My preference is 5x (Vamps & uniques too, encourages theme decks)

This would allow 5 Tombs and 5 RTIs in a 60 card deck. Does not seem like
much of a restriction to me. With Tombs and RTI's running at $15 a pop,
it would still be card lords and big spenders who are most likely to win
tournaments.

Or, at least, it was this way before recent fixes which balanced such
cards. I feel that the changes promote a game that rewards creativity and
skill more than wallet size.

In article <01bdd256$8c12baa0$0100a8c0@lurch>,
"Dog" <warp...@biosys.net> wrote:

My background first. I've played OL (the ownership limit where all of us
were just starting and so we didn't have more than four of anything anyway)
for a year, 4CL for a year with the Vienna group, 6CL for 1.5 years with
a group back in the States, and currently NL with my newest group for about 3
months. Bear in mind that these times include hiatuses once in a while
as I've been playing since Nov 94.

> I'm afraid the 7/7 rulings are the final nail in the coffin.
> The rules-team can't be trusted to make rulings.

It takes a stake through the heart to immobilize a vampire, and
beheading, fire, or sunlight to kill it.

> The claim which has ultimately led us here is that the game was designed to
> be played 'unlimited'.

Hey James, have you got that section of the FAQ done yet?

> This is ridiculous.

No kidding. Someone comes onto the newsgroup and starts arguing for
card limits with what would appear to be no prior knowledge of the debates
that have gone on before. Errrr, sorry, you were referring to the claim
that the game was designed as NL.

> Jyhad hasn't been designed with **anywhere near** the care and balance
> necessary to achieve this!

The original set is very balanced. It's only the expansions that introduce
any kind of unbalance. And even this unbalance is limited to a very small
number of cards.

> Let's take a look at just 2 of the stunning rulings which have been
> necessitated by this money-grubbing farce...

Money-grubbing? With NL, you can go out and buy boxes of Jyhad boosters
($10 each) to get all the Majesties, Earth Melds, and a few Freak Drives
as you could ever want. In terms of repeat actions, I'd hardly call
NL a money grubbing move.

> 1. The No-Repeat rulings:

> Let's call them what they really are...
> No repeat BLEED rulings!

It's not a ruling for one thing. It's part of the DCI Tournament
floor rules for Jyhad. And it prevents the repeating of a lot more
actions than just bleeding which you apparently misunderstood.

> Anson can call conservative agitation, then kine resources contested.

My reading of the clarification of the NRA rule would indicate that
he cannot. A political action is defined in the rulebook as a type of
action. Therefore, it cannot be repeated. This is the second bullet
on the web page below.

http://madnessnetwork.hexagon.net/madness_tourney_format.html

> But he can't bleed with legal manipulations, then with computer hacking.

> i.e. 'Bleed actions' are a class, but politicals aren't

> It's can't be inferred from the rulebook (unless you're a Malkie)

A political action is a type of action just as Employing a Retainer,
Bleeding, Hunting, or Recruiting an Ally. Therefore, you cannot repeat
them.

> It's purely because the unlimited game is unbalanced by repeat-bleeding.

> Experience shows that with a card limit this indefensible ruling (which
> hurts many good decks) is unnecessary.

And a CL hurts many more good decks.

> 2. The incredible 7/7 edits:
> Surely ALL of these cards can't be broken?
> We've been playing pulled fangs for half a decade, AND NOW IT'S TOO
> POWERFUL???
> Yeah.
> Right.

When you have a change of administration from a group of people that
rarely play the game and don't care much about it to a group of people
that play the game often and care a lot about it, this sort of "fixing"
is going to happen.

> With a card-limit none of these cards is broken.

O contrare, mon fraire. (yeah, I know, I butchered that.) Just because
you don't draw it more often doesn't make it any less screwed up.

> It's my impression that advocates of no-limit most often:
> 1. Make money from the industry, and are thus only interested in increasing
> sales

I have yet to know a person that uses NL and is in the industry. Heck,
many of them are on very limited funds.

> 2. Have a large collection, and wish to increase the benefit of that
> advantage in tournament play

This is the problem with impressions; they often are wrong. There are
far more players who never play in tournaments than those that do.
And a CL is more of a disadvantage to a person with fewer cards. I'll
explain below.

> I dislike *any* kind of limit on our game, but the rulings which must
> result from unlimited decks are vastly more restrictive than a simple card
> limit could ever be!

So by your argument, you'd rather remove a whole strategy from the game
(Setite Corruption) than fix only the problem cards?

> I'd really appreciate reasoned responses from any advocates of no-limits,
> if you're in the industry please admit it.

I'm not in the industry. I don't even support the industry because I
haven't bought anything more than a booster pack in over a year. You
are apparently not aware of the significant portions of old NL vs CL
discussions.

http://www.io.com/~mlangsdo/RPGs/Jyhad/index.html

> Jyhad is NOT played by morons.

No, it's not. That's why we can have reasonable discussions.

> Players should be able to decide for themselves if the unlimited position
> can be defended, or if it's a marketing ploy and should be discarded for
> our better enjoyment of the game.

It is quite defensible as you'll see on the above web site.

> If there's support I want this to be a starting place to challenge the
> international tournament rules.

There will always be people who play with CL. But their numbers are
in the minority. By how much, I don't know.

> In the last 5 years I've run 17 weekend tournaments, the biggest involved
> 34 players

I'm guessing you mistyped this since Jyhad has only been around since
1994.

> I've got a modest collection of about 30000 cards

30,000 cards? Yeesh. That's hardly modest. I'd approximate my collection
at 5,000 maximum. I've got fully 1/6 the number of cards you do, and I
advocate NL.

> The card limited games I've played range from 4x-6x
> My preference is 5x (Vamps & uniques too, encourages theme decks)

And NL encourages even more theme decks.

> The above comments are on the basis of thousands of card-limited games
> against rabid Jyhad nutters.

So you are saying that you've never played NL? I've played several
ways with NL being the shortest time span. I've based my comments on
experience as well. You can theorize all you want, but it's this kind
of experience that proves the point.

I've seen many more theme decks that were as competitive as a good
S&B deck under NL. I've played under CL quite a bit, and I definitely
cannot say the same for it. Under NL, I've seen Setite Corruption,
Lasombra Stealth/Rush/Vote/Bleed, Ravnos Steal-blood-from-vampires-in-
uncontrolled-region, a Milicent Smith/Reversal of Fortune/Eagle's Sight,
and any number of other weird discipline combinations. With a CL,
constructing these decks is sometimes absolutely impossible. A Setite
Corruption deck is only going to be able to steal a 4 capacity vampire,
assuming it draws all 4 of its Corruptions. A Ravnos Trick of Danya deck
is only going to be able to do its special 4 times.

As you know, commons are the most useful cards in Jyhad. By limiting
people to only a given number of them, you are requiring them to own
more cards in order to make the kind of deck they want. How is this
possible, you ask? Well, rather than being able to use 8 Majesties for
combat defense, you have to use 4 Majesties and 4 Catatonic Fear. You
can't get both cards in the same kind of booster, and Catatnoic Fear
is Uncommon instead of Common like Majesty. A combat deck that needs
to fight S:CE has only 4 Immortal Grapples and 4 Psyches while a Presence
using S:CE defense could have 4 Catatonic Fear, 4 Majesty, 4 Mercy for
the Weak, and 4 Staredown.

Now with that knowledge that commons are the most useful, what could
you do with those 30,000 cards? You could give those commons that you
have so many of to the players that don't want to buy their own boxes
of Jyhad. I do that with vampires as I only keep 2 of most.

And meanwhile, you've still got your 4 Tomb of Ramses III while the
player with only a handful of cards might have 1.

Read the archive at Mark Langsdorf's page above, and you'll see more
arguments for NL with 2 articles for CL.

Now I'm not saying that CL sucks or trying to tell you how to play
your game. But if you want to argue for one or the other, at least come
prepared and don't use old arguments that have already been shown to
be without merit. Although the NL being a scheme to get people to buy
more cards is a new one, but it is amusing at best.

Mike

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Dog (warp...@biosys.net) wrote:
: I'm afraid the 7/7 rulings are the final nail in the coffin.

: The rules-team can't be trusted to make rulings.

That's a strange thing to say now, considering that the rules team
hasn't supported card limits for quite a long time. (In fact, I don't
think the Rules Team ever actually supported card limits; there was
briefly a set of tournament rules that included limits on certain cards.)

: The claim which has ultimately led us here is that the game was designed to
: be played 'unlimited'.
: This is ridiculous.
: Jyhad hasn't been designed with **anywhere near** the care and balance
: necessary to achieve this!

*Jyhad* was designed with *exactly* that much care and balance. Did you
see any mention of card limits in the Jyhad rulebook? Shouldn't they
have been there if the designers intended them, considering that Magic
had had a card limit for something like a year by then? (The later
expansions did have some balance troubles, but card limits still weren't
a good answer.)

: Let's take a look at just 2 of the stunning rulings which have been

: necessitated by this money-grubbing farce...

: 1. The No-Repeat rulings:

: Let's call them what they really are...
: No repeat BLEED rulings!

As my estimable colleague pointed out, this is not true. The no-repeat-
actions rule applies to all classes of actions, including 'political
action', 'hunt', 'equip', etc. (Anson is not allowed to call KRC and
then call Conservative Agitation on the same turn.)

: 2. The incredible 7/7 edits:

: Surely ALL of these cards can't be broken?
: We've been playing pulled fangs for half a decade, AND NOW IT'S TOO
: POWERFUL???
: Yeah.
: Right.

: With a card-limit none of these cards is broken.

Tomb of Rameses III sure is. Return to Innocence sure is. If you haven't
found them to be broken, either you have a very different definition of
broken or you haven't tried to break them.

There are certainly some changes that aren't *necessary* for balancing
the game, Pulled Fangs among them. But they are *beneficial* to game
balance, because the cards in question (PF especially) are overpowered.

: It's my impression that advocates of no-limit most often:

: 1. Make money from the industry, and are thus only interested in increasing
: sales

: 2. Have a large collection, and wish to increase the benefit of that
: advantage in tournament play

I'm not in the industry. In fact, I don't think anyone makes much
money from Jyhad anymore. It just doesn't sell enough.

I have a large collection relative to someone new to the game, but not
relative to (for example) you. ;-) I probably have somewhere in the
realm of two thousand to four thousand cards.

It's also been my experience that card limits enhance the usefulness
of spending lots of money on cards more than no-limits does. This
is because in card-limit games, it is more useful to have the maximum
number of the good rares available to use, whereas in no-limit games
commons will often do just as well. (ex: someone with a small collection
is more likely to be able to get 10 Undead Strength than 5 Undead Strength
and 5 Fists of Death.)

: I dislike *any* kind of limit on our game, but the rulings which must

: result from unlimited decks are vastly more restrictive than a simple card
: limit could ever be!

Well, that's not true. You could play with a card limit *and* all
the 7/7 modifications to the cards. ;-)

: I'd really appreciate reasoned responses from any advocates of no-limits,

: if you're in the industry please admit it.

: Jyhad is NOT played by morons.
: Players should be able to decide for themselves if the unlimited position

: can be defended, or if it's a marketing ploy and should be discarded for
: our better enjoyment of the game.

Well, of course. Every player *can* decide this for himself. He can play
however he wants in the privacy of his own home. He just can't run
a DCI-sanctioned tournament with card limits.

Frankly, I don't know how you can see it as a marketing ploy, considering
that WotC hasn't been promoting this game for years now.

: If there's support I want this to be a starting place to challenge the
: international tournament rules.

But why? A lot of people like them. If your group doesn't like them,
there's nothing forcing you to use them. You can perfectly well run
tournaments using card limits; they just won't be sanctioned by the DCI.

If you haven't looked at the card limit debate archives on Mark and
Judith's web page, you might consider checking it out. There are some
good arguments put forth there, which I would just as soon not rehash
on the newsgroup if it can be avoided. (address: www.io.com/~mlangsdo/
RPGs/Jyhad/index.html#4-CARD)

: In an attempt to stave off claims I'm some whining brat here's a little
: background...

: My job is travel. I've played Jyhad in cities & towns dotted around
: Australasia.

: In the last 5 years I've run 17 weekend tournaments, the biggest involved
: 34 players
: I've got a modest collection of about 30000 cards
: The card limited games I've played range from 4x-6x

: My preference is 5x (Vamps & uniques too, encourages theme decks)

: The above comments are on the basis of thousands of card-limited games
: against rabid Jyhad nutters.

I used to play with a 4-card limit. I and my playgroup were eventually
shown the light by the discussions on this newsgroup, tried no limits,
and never went back.

Josh

ran a tournament once or twice

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Dog wrote:
"The claim which has ultimately led us here is that the game was designed to be
played 'unlimited'. This is ridiculous."

The game designers made Jyhad to be played with no card limits. Period. This
fact is not at issue. The game is very well balanced to do this, barring a few
errors that have been fixed by errata and rulings over the years. When
designing Jyhad, Garfield examined the faults in Magic and attempted to improve
upon them. Designing the game to work without card limits was one of these
major improvements.

I will grant that a handful of players _like_ to play with some sort of card
limits for various reasons (they like not having to deal with highly focused
decks, they like the diversity it promotes, whatever), and that is fine, but
Jyhad in no way _needs_ a card limit to be balanced

"Jyhad hasn't been designed with **anywhere near** the care and balance
necessary to achieve this!"

Again, barring a few minor tweaks, and the repair of some poorly designed
expansion cards, it really was.

"2. The incredible 7/7 edits:
Surely ALL of these cards can't be broken?"

Most of the edited cards were either poorly designed expansion cards (RTI,
Thoughts Betrayed, Rutor's Hand, etc.), or cards that became a bit confused in
the conversion from Jyhad to VTES and needed to be straightend out a touch.

"We've been playing pulled fangs for half a decade, AND NOW IT'S TOO
POWERFUL???"

Yup. When it was designed, it was a bit too powerful, but with the old Aggro
rules, it could never, ever, burn anyone. With the change over to VTES aggro
rules, Pulled Fangs became obscenely over powered, as it would result in a
burned vampire pretty much everytime it was played (if not, you weren't trying
hard enough). In my pretty effective Rush decks, everytime I played Pulled
Fangs, someone vanished, with no extra cost to me. This was simply too
effective, card limits or no (I was only using 4 in my deck, mind you. All
that meant was that I was only capable of burning 4 IC members per game...)

"With a card-limit none of these cards is broken."

Incorrect. A card that is too powerful is still too powerful regardless of how
many are in a deck. Having only 4 (pre 7/7) Return to Innocence in your deck
doesn't make them any less overpowered, just less likely to come up. However,
when they do come up, they are just as damaging to the game.

"It's my impression that advocates of no-limit most often:
1. Make money from the industry, and are thus only interested in increasing
sales"

Nope. The cards that you mostly need lots of are the common ones, and any CCG
player tends to have more commons than they know what to do with. How hard is
it to get, like, 10 of a common card in a group of Jyhad players? Not at all.
There are a few exceptions to this (like Immortal Grapple), but for the most
part, the cards that you tend to need more than 4 of are the common ones, not
the Rare ones.

"I dislike *any* kind of limit on our game, but the rulings which must result
from unlimited decks are vastly more restrictive than a simple card limit could
ever be!"

Any possible problem that a card limit fixes is vastly overwhelmed by the
problems caused by the card limits. For example, using a CL hamstrings to the
point of unplayability pretty much any combat deck you would card to make. As
a result of combat decks being ineffective, Stealth and Bleed decks become
_way_ too powerful and tend to dominate play, until someone decides that it is
"lame, cheezy, and unimaginitve" to play a S+B deck, and shames all of the S+B
players out of using their favored strategy. This is more effective at
balancing the game than simply playing the way it was designed?

Please, before this thread continues, I implore you to go and read all the
various articles on card limits at Mark Langsdorfs Jyhad web page (search for
Jyhad+Langsdorf--I never manage to know the URL when ever I reference his
page...). All pertinent CL arguments are archived there.

Peter D Bakija

The Hydrogen Bomb."

The claim is true. If you find that truth ridiculous, that's OK.

Richard Garfield (and WotC in general) learned a lesson from
Magic: the Gathering. That lesson was that card availability
(which they had relied on in the first few releases of MtG) was
not the hindereance they thought it would be. They had not
expected players (individually) to buy hundreds (indeed,
thousands) of dollars worth of cards.

But the players did. And the concept of using rarity (card
availability) to balance cards was abandoned.

For MtG, it was too late to re-create all of the cards, so
a card limit was introduced to (somewhat) simulate the
environement that the designers had intended.

That was well before Jyhad. When designing Jyhad, Garfield
knew that card availability couldn't be used in the balancing
equations, so all of the cards (commons and rares alike)
were *designed* to be balanced with each other.

> necessary to achieve this!

I could just point you to my web site (and I will,
http://www.io.com/~mlangsdo/RPGs/Jyhad/ ) but I'm going to summarize the
NL arguments. You can respond reasonably to them. There's a $40 stake
for a reasonable rebuttal that actually addresses these points.

Reasons why there shouldn't be a card limit in Jyhad:
(Most of these comments are cribbed from arguments by Curt Adams
and Alan Kwan. I miss Curt!)

Permanents, Transients, and Ephemerals
Cards can be roughly classified by how long their effects last.
Permanent
cards (like guns) hang around for the rest of the game, and you need
roughly 1-2 per minion. Transient cards (action or action modifiers) get
used once per action, and while you need plenty of them, too many will
choke a deck. Ephemeral cards are cards that are used more than once
per action, like most combat cards.
A 4CL is hardly a limit on Permanent cards, because most people don't
put much than 4 of any permanent card in their deck, anyway. It hurts on
transient cards, but if there's enough duplication in the card set, you can
(to some extent) get around it. It cripples Ephemerals.
So the 1st problem with CL play is that it has differing effects on
different strategies. If you play with a lot of permanents (bleed decks,
maybe) then it doesn't hurt you too much. If you play with a lot of
transients (vote decks, certainly) than you begin to have problems. If
you play with a lot of ephemerals (combat, combat, combat!) then
you've been hosed.

Unequal Effects on Disciplines and Strategies
Some disciplines have a lot of overlap in their card effects: for
example,
Obfuscate and Dominate, where there are lots of cards with similar
abilities. Other disciplines have very diverse effects (Animalism,
Chimestry)
that aren't duplicated. What other card works like Drawing Out the Beast?
How does Presence vote work with only 4 Bewitching Orations?
The 2nd problem with a CL is that some disciplines are mostly unaffected
(because they use transients and have a lot of overlap) and that others
are almost entirely unusable (because they have little overlap and use
ephemerals).

Domination of Certain Archetypes
The first two problems combine into a big third problem. Since the
bleed strategy is less affected by card limits than others, and dominate
and obfuscate are less affected than others, Malkavian S&B is still
fairly playable under a CL. (Boring, maybe, but playable). On the
other hand, other deck archetypes (Brujah Rush, Settite Corruption)
are fairly to completely hosed. So Jyhad becomes a question of "Did
two people bring a Malk deck?" instead of deck construction and
play skill. People either play Malk S&B (or one of its cousins, like
Lasombra S&B) or a defense against Malk S&B (Malk or Tremere
bleed bounce or intercept).

Death of Deck Variety
A CL also makes it impossible to play certain kinds of decks.
There is 1 Potence anti-S:CE (Immortal Grapple), there are about
12 different S:CEs. A lot of potence combats will get cut short,
with no fear for the minion playing S:CE. Potence pitch (throw
stuff) decks also have a problem: 4 Gates, 4 Lids, 4 Sacraments,
and... well, nothing. Settite Corruption is impossible. Offensive
Intercept (using Eagle's Sight to block your prey's bleed actions)
is impossible. Princely Intercept (using 2nd Tradition: Domain to
block actions) becomes impossible. And so.
So the 4th problem with a CL is that it makes large numbers of
interesting and non-abusive decks non-viable. (Granted, it makes
a few decks that aren't viable under NL viable. But you're losing
more than you're gaining).

Mr. Suitcase and the Industry
Card limits are supposed to even the playing field for new players,
since people with lots of cards can't use all those rares unfairly
against the new players. Unfortunately, since Jyhad is a game of
commons, the CL works the other way.
Dominate Kine is a rare card that lets a minion bleed at +2
bleed and +2 stealth - it's roughly the equivalent of a Govern
the Unaligned and a Lost in Crowds. In NL play, if a new player
wants to build a bleed deck, she can trade her 1 DK to Mr. Suitcase
for a fistful of Governs and Losts and build a bleed deck. In
4CL play, she can put in 4 Governs and 4 Lost in Crowds - while
Mr. Suitcase can do the same _and_ put in 4 DKs.
The 5th problem with a CL is that it punishes people with smaller
collections, who can't get multiple couples of the rare cards with
similar effects to the common cards. In order to play competively,
players have to buy additional boxes to get more cards.

Infrequently Broken is Still Broken
Finally, a card limit is supposed to cure the abusiveness of
certain cards, such as Return to Innocence or Tomb of Ramses
III. But whether I play 1 ToR3 or 5 in a game, the fact is, I get
more from the Tomb than I paid for it, and I didn't have to
risk anything to get it out or to make a profit from it. The single
RtI I get off in a game still ousts my prey, even though he was
sitting pretty at 10 blood. The cards are still broken, Nothing
was fixed.
The 6th problem with a CL is that it doesn't fix broken cards -
it just makes the abuses less frequent.

6 logical, reasonable, and cool-blooded arguments against a
card limit and for no-limit play.
Rebuttal to you, sir.

Mark Langsdorf
Jyhad Archivist
http://www.io.com/~mlangsdo/RPGs/Jyhad

He's got some good points, too.

Subject: The Compleat NRA (Re: LSJ:? Numerous Questions)

***

First, a quote from the DCI rules (July 1, 1997):

1. Repeat Action rule: No single vampire can repeat an action in a
turn.
This refers to the particular action type. For example, a vampire
which
successfully bleeds its prey via Computer Hacking, then untaps via
Freak
Drive, cannot perform any bleeding action again whatsoever that turn,
regardless of whether or not it is a Computer Hacking action.

Note: the word "vampire" in the first sentence should be "minion".

Implementation is complicated by two things: timing (only really
interesting in cases like Mask of a Thousand faces where the acting
minion changes) and figuring out what constitutes the same "type of
action".

The easy one first: Timing.

Implementation of NRA can be viewed as a restriction the acting
minion receives. The restriction is applied when the action
resolves (that is, when it ends, either successful or not). Only
the acting minion at that time gets the restriction (not any
prior acting minion, in the case that the action was taken over
by some new minion playing Mask of a Thousand Faces).

The second one is addressed by simply defining what the different types
of actions are:

1) Action types defined in the rulebook (6.4, 7, and 19)
These are:
* Bleed
* Hunt
* Employ (Retainer)
* Recruit (Ally)
* Equip
* Transfer Equipment
* Call a vote
* Leave Torpor
* Rescue (from Torpor)
* Diablerize (in Torpor)

2) Actions allowed by action cards that are not covered above.
Every action card is of the "type" of its card name.
Examples: Bum's Rush, Army of Rats (putting into play), Far
Mastery.

3) Actions allowed by cards in play that are not covered by 1).
Each of these is a distinct type per card in play. So each
Haven Uncovered provides a unique action type (to attack the
target vampire), even though the cards have the same name.

***

Why should I be forced to use Lightning Reflexes instead of Blur? I
don't want to pay three blood for two additional strikes from one card
when I can pay one.

Why can't I have a lot of Backstab cards in my Toreador intercept deck?
I want to be able to hit you first so I can aggravated damage to you
before you hit me. Why can't I do that?

Why can't I have a lot of Bewitching Oration cards in my deck? I want
to pass my votes using Presence. I don't want to give other people pool
with Bribes because I want to be weakening them, not giving them pool.

Why do I have to stop using Skin of Steel to prevent your strikes? Why
should I have to use Skin of Rock instead when I might need several of
them?

I want to set aside some room for stealth in my deck - say, 20 cards.
And I want them from Obfuscate too. I don't have any other stealth
disciplines in my deck. The decisions that I, as an NL player, have to
make are far more complicated than the decisions that a CL player has to
make. Do I want to go for 8 of one stealth card? The superiors can
make that difference if I want to fail your blocking attempts, tap you
regardless, get more stealth, maneuver or whatever.

>
>I'd really appreciate reasoned responses from any advocates of no-limits,
>if you're in the industry please admit it.

No-one who posts regularly on this group is working for WotC (in a
financial sense), even LSJ, as far as I know. A few WotC employees post
from time to time (Matt Green of Wizards UK, say) but rarely get caught
up in arguments - they don't have the time, usually. No-one on this
group benefits financially from V:TES directly, except in the fringe
area of maybe selling people their cards if they can't come up with a
trade or whatever.

>Jyhad is NOT played by morons.

You what? You think that just because someone plays Jyhad they are not
a moron? Sorry to disillusion you mate, there are dingbats out there
who play Jyhad too.

>Players should be able to decide for themselves if the unlimited position
>can be defended,

It can. It stands up for itself quite nicely all the time. If it
didn't, it wouldn't be the official way to play the game. The official
way to play the game is now NOT set by a company getting money from the
game. It is now set by a player consulting with other players as to the
best way to play the game.

I would suggest you look for the Judith and Mark Jyhad page (the URL
escapes me but you can search for that in Yahoo et al). Plenty of
arguments for NL there which you might like to peruse.

For me, the driving parts of the argument for NL are:

1) Choice - why should an arbitrary limit dictate how I build my decks
to me? If I want a deck with 35 copies of Cryptic Mission in it (ackn.
Robert Goudie), why shouldn't I be allowed to have them?

2) Utility - some cards AREN'T useful if I can only have x of them -
where x is between 4 and 6. Corruption is a good example. Bewitching
Oration is another - Awe isn't a replacement for BewOra, it's an
alternative which has different requirements and abilities.

3) Inherent restrictions - you can't play more than one of a named
action modifier on action with one minion, similar with reactions.
You're limited as to how many action cards you can feasibly have in a
deck by the number of minions you're likely going to have to play them.
You're limited by expensive pool costs which take away from your pool,
taking you closer to a striking distance for your opponent to hit you
and you keel over. You're limited as to the number of master cards you
can feasibly have in a deck by the number you can play in a turn.

4) Similar Cards - There are almost no cards in Jyhad which are an exact
copy of another - none, as far as I know. There is no way, with a Card
Limit, to get another card which does an exact copy of what I want it
to. Take the cards Claws of the Dead, Wolf Claws and Bone Spur. All
three are identical at inferior I believe, but at superior, *I* start
making choices. What do I value more? Do I value the ability to
maneuver more than press? Would I prefer the remainder of the combat?
In my taste, I prefer Claws of the Dead. I prefer the ability to be
able to maneuver in a pinch - even if it does cost me a blood. So if I
wanted to put 15 claw cards in a deck (a not unreasonable number), I
would probably put 10 Claws of the Dead and 5 Wolf Claws. I don't like
Bone Spur's superior - it simply wouldn't be useful in my deck. Under
xCL, though, to get 15 claws, I'd have to start putting them all in -
even if I didn't want them. If it was 4CL, I wouldn't necessarily be
able to get 15 claw cards in the deck!

> or if it's a marketing ploy and should be discarded for
>our better enjoyment of the game.

Did you ever do any Business Studies? If you did, you'd know that if No
Limits was intended as a marketing ploy, it was stunningly unsuccessful.
Jyhad is a small game, with dedicated players. It is not making vast
amounts of money for WotC. If it was, we'd be getting new expansions
all the time.

Enjoyment of the game is a very subjective term. In your own games,
play however you want. If you preferred flicking the cards at each
other and trying to give each other long range paper cuts, that'd be
fine - but just because you enjoyed it wouldn't necessarily make it
suitable for tournament rules.

The only problems I've ever found with NL are that broken cards may turn
up more often. If you don't have the broken cards, any environment
benefits if you work on the premise that broken cards are bad for the
game - which I do.

>If there's support I want this to be a starting place to challenge the
>international tournament rules.

This is the place where the tournament rules are challenged. Basically
always has been, because it's been the place to liaise with netreps, and
now, the official rules setter.

Please, just because *you* play Card Limits, it doesn't mean the rest of
us have to. In your own games, you can play whatever you want. No-one
will stop you. It's your game to play however you want in your house.

If you want to play DCI, you have to play the official rules. The
official rules are based *now* on several things:

1) The original intent of the game/cards being preserved if possible
2) The original intent of the game/cards being thrown out of the window
if it busts the game
3) Rules/errata/clarifications being introduced to stop the game being
bust if it becomes a problem

NCL is not a problem. It does not bust the game. If you believe it
does, you haven't played it enough.

>The above comments are on the basis of thousands of card-limited games
>against rabid Jyhad nutters.

*sigh*

Based on lots of card limited games. How many NCL games have you
played? NCL is perfectly fine in and of itself. Plenty of players from
many different groups who will attest to that on this newsgroup if you
want.

If you agree that a ruling/errata/clarification for a card would be
needed under NCL, then it is very difficult to argue for its dropping
under xCL. Okay, let's take hypothetical card X. Now, X is a very
powerful card *somehow* so the errata/clarifications/whatever alter the
way in which it works to something acceptable, okay? This is fine. A
few people will argue "But that's how I want the card" or "You've
devalued a card I went out and bought" or whatever. But the card was
generally agreed to be bust and so was toned down to an acceptable
level.

In NCL, I could put quite a few of Card X in my deck. It meant that I
drew it regularly, and so could abuse it more times.

In xCl, I could put x of Card X in my deck. It meant that I drew it
less regularly, but it didn't stop it being bust when I drew it. I
could still abuse Card X to my heart's content, I just had it a smaller
amount of times.

Why does having fewer of a card in a deck stop the card being broken?
Is there something about having more of a card in a deck that suddenly
makes it become broken? Does it suddenly become more powerful by magic,
because there are more of it in a deck? No, a card is broken because it
is broken. The number you have in a deck is irrelevant, it's still
broken.

I've had decks where I've had one copy of Return to Innocence in them.
The rest of the deck was a fairly weird Protean-Dominate deck - bit of
bleed, bit of stealth, bit of claw, bit of GraveRob. However, in the
first game, I drew Return to Innocence. Ousted my prey within about 20
minutes, because I stealthed the bleed past (he was playing Assamites).
And I only had one copy of the card in my deck.

I believe RtoI to be bust. Just because I had one copy of it in my deck
didn't make it any less bust. If there are cards that you believe to be
bust under NL, I will argue that there are just as bust under xCL, you
just don't pull them as often.

I only need one copy of RtoI in my hand, what does it matter if there
are another 4 copies of it in the deck or another 10?

Dog wrote:
"You're trying to put words in my mouth :-o
I said it hasn't been *designed* to be played unlimited."

Again, this is so far from correct that the light from correct will take a
billion years to reach it. From the beginning, Jyhad was designed specifically
and intentionally to be played with no card limits. Magic was designed to be
played where card rarity and availablitily was a _severe_ game environment
condition. This turned out to be a complete failure (in that the game became
far more popular than the designers could have possibly imagined), and as a
result, artificial means of imposing this environment had to be
implimented-card limits. In light of this, Jyhad was designed in such a way
that the game would work with no card limits, so that card availiblity and
rarity were not taken into consideration as a balancing point, and players
could actually benefit from having 10 of each rare (as opposed to Magic, where
commons possessed over the needed 4 are regularly thrown away to make space for
more cards).

"Fact: Numerous rule changes have been (and continue to be) made to
compensate for imbalances which cripple unlimited Jyhad
Conclusion: Lack of appropriate design"

This is completely wrong. Wrong, wrong, wrong. The only two rules that have
been imposed to repair basic flaws with the game of Jyhad are:

1) No vote pushing-The "throw all the votes you want to pass a vote" rule was
damaging to the play environment, as it made WVP decks way too effective. It
is arguable that the rules were originally designed to play the way they
currently do, and that the unrestricted vote push rules were, in fact, an
error, and as such the 7/7 rules exist to restore the game to where it should
have been from the get go. As such, this is not a "rules change made to
compensate for imbalances that cripple unlimited Jyhad."

2. No repeat actions. Repeat actions were an unforseen flaw in the game. Ok.
I'll accept that. NRA, however, aren't even an official general rule, only
required for tournament play.

All other rules changes and errata are minor tweaks of cards that became a bit
confused between Jyhad and VTES, or were designed poorly (Magic does this all
the time, sometimes by errata, usually by reprinting fixed versions of the
cards. Lighting bolt and Shock? Shatter and Shattering Pulse?)

"You could play baseball with a brick.
But it'd detract from the game."

I assure you that playing Jyhad with card limits has a _far_ greater deletrious
effect on the game as a whole than any possible rules tweaking.

"Incidentally I don't really care about the classifications, I'm much more
interested in the underlying reason for the No Repeat rule."

You are correct. The basis for the No Repeat Actions rule is not in the
rulebook by any stretch of the imagination, any more than "Classic" and
"Restricted" deck types have a basis in the rule book in Magic. This does not
make the NRA rules any less valid as a balancing point, however.
